title: PAUL HAD TO TELL A CHURCH TO STOP DEPRIVING THEIR SPOUSES SEXUALLY
paragraphs: PAUL HAD TO TELL A CHURCH TO STOP DEPRIVING THEIR SPOUSES SEXUALLY

The passage many Christians whisper about may expose something far deeper than a lack of sex: the quiet distance, rejection, resentment, selfishness, and spiritual warfare slowly entering marriages behind closed doors.
There are Bible verses people frame and hang on walls.
There are verses we underline in church.
There are verses we quote when life falls apart.
And then there are verses we almost never hear preached because everybody suddenly becomes uncomfortable.
First Corinthians 7 contains some of those verses.
Paul is writing to believers in Corinth about marriage, holiness, temptation, singleness, sexuality, and devotion to God when he says something startlingly direct.

Those words are found in 1 Corinthians 7:5. The verb translated “deprive” is apostereō—language of withholding or depriving someone of something. Paul is addressing husbands and wives who apparently needed to understand that marriage was not supposed to become a battlefield where sexual intimacy could simply be withheld unilaterally.
But before somebody weaponizes that verse against a husband or wife tonight, keep reading.
Because Paul’s message is far more beautiful—and far more demanding—than “my spouse owes me sex.”
In fact, read carefully enough and Paul destroys that selfish interpretation.
He begins this section by answering matters the Corinthians themselves had written to him about: “Περὶ δὲ ὧν ἐγράψατε”—“Now concerning the matters about which you wrote.”

Paul had already confronted sexual immorality elsewhere in the letter, but apparently another danger had emerged at the opposite extreme. Some believers seem to have been wrestling with the idea that abstaining from sexual relations was spiritually superior. Paul therefore has to explain that holiness inside marriage does not require spouses to become strangers to one another.
“The husband should give to his wife what is due her and likewise the wife to her husband.”

He says the wife does not exercise exclusive authority over her body but her husband does—and then, in a strikingly reciprocal statement, says the husband does not exercise exclusive authority over his body but his wife does.
In Greek, the repeated word is ἐξουσιάζει—exousiazei, from the language of authority.
And Paul applies the principle in both directions.
Paul is not handing husbands a divine permission slip for sexual domination. He is confronting selfishness in both spouses with radical mutuality.
“Your body belongs to me, so give me what I want.”
“I no longer live as though my desires, comfort, affection, vulnerability, and body concern only me. I have entered covenant with you, and therefore your good matters deeply to me.”
Because biblical intimacy cannot be reduced to taking.
This is why 1 Corinthians 7:5 must never become ammunition for coercion, intimidation, manipulation, marital rape, or ignoring a spouse’s pain, trauma, illness, exhaustion, fear, or safety.
Those things are not justified by Paul’s words.
The passage itself says temporary abstinence should happen “ἐκ συμφώνου”—ek symphōnou—by agreement.
The idea behind symphōnos is agreement or harmony; it is related to the word from which English gets “symphony.”
Paul’s picture is not one spouse overpowering the other.
It is two lives learning harmony.
Two people belonging to Christ and therefore refusing to treat one another as objects.
And suddenly this uncomfortable passage becomes painfully relevant.
Because sometimes the deepest problem in a marriage is not what happens in the bedroom.
It is everything that happened before the bedroom door closed.
It was the argument nobody resolved.
The phone that became more interesting than the person sitting beside you.
The harsh words that never really left the room.
The husband who feels unwanted but is ashamed to admit it.
The wife who feels used rather than cherished but does not know how to say it.
Two people sleeping inches apart while emotionally living miles away.
Same wedding photographs hanging on the wall.
And perhaps nobody knows except them.
That is why reducing Paul's teaching to “have more sex” misses his point.
But sex cannot save a marriage.
The Gospel reaches deeper than physical intimacy because the Gospel confronts the selfish heart that damages intimacy in the first place.
Scripture tells husbands elsewhere to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her.
Christ did not exploit His bride.
Christ sacrificed Himself for His bride.
He did not say, “What can I take from you?”
That is the shadow of the cross hanging over Christian marriage.
A husband cannot appeal to biblical authority while ignoring Christlike sacrifice.
A wife cannot appeal to her husband's duty while refusing Christlike love.
Neither spouse gets permission to use intimacy as punishment.
Neither spouse gets permission to demand intimacy without tenderness.
Neither spouse gets permission to cultivate secret sexual sin and expect the marriage to remain untouched.
Neither spouse gets permission to stop caring about the heart of the person they promised to love.
Paul calls husband and wife away from selfish possession and toward mutual self-giving.
Paul says not to deprive one another except by mutual agreement “for a time,” for devotion to prayer, and afterward to come together again so Satan does not exploit their lack of self-control.
He knows marriage does not magically eliminate temptation.
And he refuses to pretend otherwise.
Paul does not say temptation excuses adultery.
He does not say a spouse’s rejection makes pornography acceptable.
He does not say sexual frustration gives anyone permission to cheat.
The answer to temptation is not blame.
And when necessary, wise pastoral or professional help.
Maybe this article hurts because your marriage has been cold for months.
Maybe you stopped touching because every touch started feeling like a request.
Maybe your spouse stopped initiating because rejection became too painful.
Maybe trauma made physical closeness complicated.
Maybe resentment entered quietly and unpacked its bags.
Maybe you cannot even remember when you stopped laughing together.
And now you are reading Paul's words thinking:
This passage was not written so wounded spouses could beat each other with Scripture.
It was written to call Christian marriages back toward covenant faithfulness.
If intimacy has become painful, frightening, coercive, medically difficult, emotionally unsafe, or tangled in trauma, the answer is not to force the verse harder.
Love does not dishonor another person.
Love does not insist on selfish gratification while ignoring another person's suffering.
And where there is abuse or sexual coercion, getting to safety and seeking qualified help is not rebellion against Scripture. Biblical submission to Christ never requires silently permitting abuse.
But for other marriages, the conviction may land differently.
Maybe intimacy has become a weapon.
“If you make me angry, I will reject you.”
“If you do not do what I want, I will punish you with distance.”
“You hurt me, so now I will make you hurt.”
And resentment can become incredibly sophisticated.
But behind the bedroom door, two hearts are keeping score.
This is where the Gospel becomes painfully practical.
Jesus did not save us merely so we could sing louder on Sunday.
He came to make dead hearts alive.
He came to expose hidden sin.
He came to teach selfish people how to love.
He came to forgive the guilty and transform the forgiven.
Maybe the prayer your marriage needs tonight is not:
“Jesus... show me where I have stopped loving.”
The years of avoiding the conversation.
But exposure in the hands of Jesus is not the end of the story.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners do not have to remain what sin has made them.
Jesus Christ was crucified for sinners and rose again.
At the cross, our deepest scandal met a deeper grace.
None of those things are stronger than the blood of Christ.
Repentance does not mean pretending the damage never happened.
Grace does not mean consequences disappear overnight.
Forgiveness does not mean trust must instantly return.
Restoration may require confession, boundaries, counseling, accountability, patience, and a long road of rebuilding what sin destroyed.
And resurrection means the grave does not get the final sentence.
Maybe your marriage will not heal because somebody finally wins the argument.
Maybe healing begins when somebody finally puts down the weapon.
“I pressured you instead of loving you.”
That is where scandal can begin turning into grace.
Not because Christians pretend everything is fine.
And rewritten people can begin rewriting patterns.
The cold room can become a place of conversation again.
The hand that stopped reaching can learn tenderness again.
The counseling appointment can finally be made.
The secret addiction can finally be dragged into the light.
The apology can finally be spoken without excuses.
The marriage that has been surviving on appearances can finally tell the truth.
And sometimes the first miracle is simply this:
Two people stop asking, “What am I owed?”
“How can I love you like Christ?”
If this exposed something hidden in you, do not rush past the conviction.
Talk honestly with your spouse where it is wise and safe.

And if your marriage needs help beyond what the two of you can repair alone, seek mature, biblically grounded pastoral counsel and qualified professional care. There is no spiritual trophy for letting serious wounds become deeper because you were too ashamed to ask for help.
Another human being cannot become your savior.

Paul himself immediately recognizes singleness as a gift from God. Scripture does not teach that everyone must marry, nor that sexual fulfillment is necessary for a meaningful Christian life. Jesus Himself shows us that perfect humanity does not require marriage or sexual activity.
So whether married or single, the center remains the same.
If you are married, love your spouse under the lordship of Christ.
If you are single, honor Christ with your body.
If you have sexually sinned, repent and run toward Christ rather than hiding from Him.
If you have been sexually wounded, know that Scripture does not give another person permission to exploit you.
If your marriage is struggling, stop protecting the image while the covenant bleeds.
Bring what is hidden into the light.
Because perhaps the most frightening thing about 1 Corinthians 7 is not that Paul talked openly about sex.
Perhaps it is that God cares about what happens in the parts of our lives we thought were too private for discipleship.
Jesus wants the Sunday version of you.
He is Lord of all of it.
Did this hit somewhere you did not expect?
And if Christ is restoring something you once thought was beyond repair, tell somebody what He has done. Your testimony may become the hope another husband or wife desperately needed tonight.
Come back to it when resentment starts speaking louder than covenant.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
But if this ministry is helping people encounter Scripture faithfully, sharing it is one practical way you can help put biblical truth in front of someone who might never search for it themselves.
Because this ministry was never supposed to terminate on a screen.
More sin brought into the light.
More wounded people pointed toward Christ.
More believers becoming disciples rather than spectators.
More people discovering that their worst chapter does not have authority to write their final one.
Because maybe tonight there is a husband staring at the ceiling beside the woman he loves, wondering when they became strangers.
Maybe there is a wife reading this with tears she does not want anyone to notice.
Maybe there is someone carrying sexual shame from years ago.
Maybe there is a marriage barely breathing beneath years of unresolved hurt.
And maybe somebody needs to hear one final truth before closing this article.
Jesus is not frightened by the room you have been afraid to let Him enter.
The same Savior who carried scandal to a cross walked out of a grave—and no chapter surrendered to Him has to remain exactly as sin wrote it.
Your marriage may have pages stained by rejection, failure, tears, and shame... but never mistake a stained page for the end of the story.
